evidence_quotes.quote: Source water protection is operationalized through land and water planning activities aimed at reducing the risk of contamination from entering a public drinking water supply. Here, we introduce a source water protection planning process at Muskowekwan First Nation, Treaty 4, Saskatchewan.

The planning process used at Muskowekwan First Nation was adapted from an established ﬁve-stage source water protection planning framework [25]. The federal government’s planning framework represents a structured, rational planning approach with the speciﬁc purpose of assisting First Nations in Canada with drinking water protection.

This was initiated at the water workshops hosted by Muskowekwan with the working committee and community members. The planning process consisted of six meetings over a twelve-month period involving the university researchers and the working committee.

Through a collaborative source water protection planning process two signiﬁcant outcomes were revealed. The ﬁrst outcome was risk aversion through adaptation strategies and management actions to protect drinking water sources.

The second outcome was the reclaiming of indigenous planning through the practice of source water protection planning. In combination, these two outcomes contribute positively and directly to building water security.

criterion_notes.c1: Fails c1: Although the paper provides background statistics on First Nations water/wastewater infrastructure and briefly inventories Muskowekwan First Nation's existing delivery modes (~90 trucked-water cistern households, 50-60 piped households, 5-6 private wells), the empirical study examines source water protection planning aimed at reducing contamination risk to untreated drinking water supplies and cisterns (water-quality/environmental planning), not household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, this paper would pass (plain=yes) because it examines a community-based participatory water governance/planning process (adapting a federal five-stage source water protection planning framework with Indigenous planning principles) framed against colonial and constitutional governance background (the Indian Act and federal-provincial jurisdictional fragmentation). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, however, it fails (narrow=no): the empirically studied exposure is participatory environmental/land-use planning and physical contamination-control project delivery (cistern cleaning, wellhead protection, well decommissioning, site remediation), not a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariffs, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure), and the Indian Act / constitutional discussion is unanalysed macro-governance background. Because the paper also fails c1 and c4, plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Passes c3: Reports primary empirical qualitative/participatory case-study evidence from a 12-month community-based participatory planning process (six working-committee workshops, water system inventory, collaborative contaminant risk-ranking matrix, and initial implementation tracking) at Muskowekwan First Nation.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails c4: Reported outcomes are (1) risk rankings of 23 potential contaminant threats and initiation of physical contamination-mitigation actions (cistern cleaning/repair, wellhead protection, well decommissioning, diesel shed remediation) and (2) reclaiming of Indigenous planning (cultural identity, self-determination, and local planning capacity). No outcome measuring household or community water/sanitation access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Passes c5: The community population and working committee, participatory planning exposure, contamination-risk/empowerment outcomes, and community-based participatory case-study design are clearly identifiable, though the topic, exposure, and outcomes fall outside review scope.
criterion_notes.c6: Passes c6: Full text is in English.

population_and_sample: Muskowekwan First Nation community in Treaty 4, Saskatchewan, Canada (~500 on-reserve residents across ~90 trucked-water cistern households, 50-60 piped households, and 5-6 private-well households; multi-stakeholder working committee across six workshops over 12 months)
exposure: Adapted five-stage community-based participatory source water protection planning process
outcome: Contaminant threat risk rankings and physical contamination-mitigation actions (cistern cleaning/repair, wellhead protection, well decommissioning, diesel-shed remediation), plus reclaiming of Indigenous planning (cultural identity, empowerment, and local planning capacity)
rationale: Exclude (E01: Wrong topic; also fails c2 narrow rule-type exposure and c4 access outcome). While the introduction discusses First Nations water infrastructure and colonial/constitutional water governance as background, the empirical study is a community-based participatory source water protection planning case study focused on identifying drinking-water contamination threats and initiating physical contamination-prevention actions (cistern cleaning, wellhead protection, well decommissioning, site remediation) alongside cultural empowerment. It does not examine water or sanitation service access (c1=no), does not evaluate a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope (c2=no; participatory contamination planning passes plain c2 wording as governance, but fails narrow rule-type scope), and reports no service-access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (c4=no; hence plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude).
